title: What a sound wave is, and how to read its formula
summary: Say what a waveform shows; find period, frequency and amplitude on a plot; read A, F and ϕ off A·cos(2πFt + ϕ); change one number and predict the new plot; know what a spectrum is.
sourceNote: basic_acoustics.pdf (Day 2), sinusoids_review.pdf and basic_sinusoids.pdf (Day 3), Lab 1, Lab 3 Q1–Q4. Rewritten in plain steps: one idea per card.

sections.heading: The whole course on one page

blocks.md: **Read this first.** LING 124 is about one question: *how does a computer turn a recording of speech into text?* Every day of the course is one step of that trip. If you know which step you're on, the math has a reason.
blocks.label: why

rows: Sound is air pressure going up and down. We draw it as a wave.
The computer measures that wave thousands of times a second and stores the numbers.
Any sound can be split into simple waves added together.
We cut the recording into tiny slices and find the simple waves in each slice.
From each slice we measure pitch and a short list of numbers that describe the sound.
A model reads those numbers and guesses the words.
blocks.title: Speech to text, in six steps
blocks.slide: Six steps from sound to text

blocks.md: You don't need to understand all six now. Just come back to this table whenever you feel lost and find the row you're on.

blocks.body: Air pressure going up and down, very fast. When you talk, your vocal folds push air in little puffs; the pressure rises and falls, and that ripple travels to someone's ear.

blocks.md: **Picture it.** Drop a stone in a pond: the water goes up and down, and the ripple moves outward. Sound is the same thing, but in air, and far too fast to see.

blocks.body: A graph of that pressure over time. Left to right is **time**. Up and down is **pressure** (how much the air is squeezed or stretched). Every recording you open in Audacity or Praat is a waveform.

blocks.prompt: On a waveform, what does the horizontal axis show, and what does the vertical axis show?

sections.heading: Three numbers that describe a wave

blocks.md: A simple wave repeats the same shape over and over. You only need three numbers to describe it. Learn them one at a time.

blocks.body: How long **one** repeat takes, in seconds. If the wave repeats every 0.01 seconds, T = 0.01 s (that's 10 milliseconds).
How many repeats happen **in one second**. Measured in **Hertz (Hz)**. 100 Hz = 100 repeats per second.

blocks.title: Period and frequency are flips of each other
blocks.body:
If one repeat takes 0.01 s, how many fit in 1 second?
  1 ÷ 0.01 = 100 repeats → F = 100 Hz

So:  F = 1 / T   and   T = 1 / F

  T = 0.5 s   →  F = 2 Hz
  T = 0.002 s →  F = 500 Hz
  F = 200 Hz  →  T = 1/200 = 0.005 s = 5 ms

blocks.prompt: A wave has F = 250 Hz. What is its period in milliseconds?

blocks.body: How far the wave goes up from the middle line. A bigger amplitude means more pressure change, which sounds louder. If the wave goes up to 3 and down to −3, the amplitude is 3.
**Periodic** = repeats the same shape (vowels like *aa*, a tuning fork, a hum). **Aperiodic** = no repeating shape (*s*, *sh*, static).

blocks.prompt: Is the sound 'sss' periodic or aperiodic?
blocks.answer: Aperiodic: it's a hiss with no repeating shape.

blocks.md: **Loudness in decibels (dB).** Our ears don't hear loudness in a straight line: doubling the pressure does not sound twice as loud. So we use a scale that counts **how many times bigger**, called decibels. You only need two facts:

blocks.title: The formula (only if you need it)
blocks.body:
dB = 20 · log₁₀(new amplitude ÷ old amplitude)

Example: amplitude goes from 0.3 to 0.6.
  ratio = 0.6 ÷ 0.3 = 2
  20 · log₁₀(2) = 20 · 0.301 ≈ 6 dB louder

blocks.prompt: Sound B's amplitude is 10 times sound A's. How many dB louder is B?

sections.heading: Where the wave shape comes from: a dot going around a circle

blocks.md: **Picture it.** Imagine a dot going around a circle, like the tip of a clock hand going the wrong way. Now watch only its **left-right position**. It slides right, back to the middle, left, back to the middle, right again… Plot that position over time and you get the wave shape. That shape is called a **cosine**.

blocks.slide: The shadow of a rotating point

blocks.body: The dot's **left-right** position. It starts at 1 (far right), goes to 0, −1, 0, and back to 1 after one full lap.
The dot's **up-down** position. Same shape as cosine, just a quarter lap later.
A way to measure angles. One full lap is **2π radians** (about 6.28). Half a lap is π. A quarter lap is π/2.

blocks.md: **Why this matters:** after a full lap (2π), the dot is back where it started. So adding 2π to the angle changes nothing. That fact answers a lot of lab questions (Lab 3 Q3).

blocks.prompt: What is cos(π)? Picture the dot.
blocks.answer: −1. At π (half a lap) the dot is on the far left.

sections.heading: The wave formula, one piece at a time

blocks.md: Every simple wave in this course is written like this: **A · cos(2π · F · t + ϕ)**. It looks scary, but it is just the dot on the circle with three dials. Let's build it one piece at a time.

frames.caption: Start with the plain wave shape. θ (the Greek letter theta) is just an angle: how far the dot has gone around the circle. cos(θ) goes 1, 0, −1, 0, 1 as θ goes once around.

Make it move in time. F is how many laps the dot makes per second, and one lap is 2π. So after t seconds the angle is 2π·F·t. Example: F = 2 laps per second, after t = 1 second the dot has gone 2 laps = 4π.
Make it taller or shorter. cos only goes from −1 to 1. Multiply by A and it goes from −A to A. A is the amplitude.
Give it a head start. ϕ (the Greek letter phi, say 'fye') is the angle the dot starts at when t = 0. ϕ = 0 means it starts at the top of the wave.

lines: A = how tall   F = how fast   ϕ = where it starts   t = the clock
frames.caption: That's the whole formula. Three dials (A, F, ϕ) and a clock (t). Every sinusoid in this course is this formula with different numbers.

rows: where in its cycle the wave starts
blocks.title: The three dials

frames.caption: Lab 3's formula. Find the three dials.
The number in front: amplitude 2. The wave swings between −2 and +2.
The number right before t (after the 2π): 100 laps per second, so 100 Hz. The 2π is NOT part of the frequency.
The number added at the end: the starting angle, π/3 (that's 60°).
Bonus: once you have F you have the period, T = 1/F.

blocks.body: Saying the frequency is 2π·100 = 628. The 2π is just there because one lap is 2π. The frequency is the number right before t: **100 Hz**.

blocks.title: Turn one dial at a time
blocks.body:
Start:  3·cos(2π·5·t)

Change A: 10·cos(2π·5·t)       → same wave, taller (±10 instead of ±3)
Change F: 3·cos(2π·10·t)       → twice as many repeats, squished sideways
Add ϕ = π: 3·cos(2π·5·t + π)   → flipped: starts at the bottom instead of the top

blocks.prompt: Write a wave with amplitude 0.5 and frequency 440 Hz that starts at the top.
blocks.answer: 0.5 · cos(2π · 440 · t). Starting at the top means ϕ = 0.

blocks.prompt: Write the same wave but starting at the bottom.
blocks.answer: 0.5 · cos(2π · 440 · t + π). Half a lap (π) head start puts the dot on the far left, so the wave starts at its lowest point.

blocks.md: **Lab 3 Q3 tip:** two formulas are the same wave if their starting angles differ by a whole number of laps (±2π, ±4π…). Example: ϕ = π/3 and ϕ = π/3 − 2π = −5π/3 are the same starting point.

sections.heading: A spectrum: the recipe of a sound

blocks.md: **The big idea.** Real sounds (like a vowel) are not one simple wave. They are **many simple waves added together**. A **spectrum** is the recipe: which simple waves are in the sound, and how much of each.
**Picture it.** A smoothie tastes like one thing, but it's made of ingredients: some banana, a lot of strawberry, a little milk. A spectrum is the ingredient list for a sound.

rows: which frequencies are in it, and how strong (one moment)
how the spectrum changes over time
blocks.title: Three plots you'll see all semester

blocks.body: The simple waves that make up a vowel sit at evenly spaced frequencies: F₀, 2·F₀, 3·F₀… F₀ (say 'F-zero') is the lowest one, and it's the **pitch** of the voice.
The big bumps in a vowel's spectrum. They come from the shape of your mouth, and they're what make *ee* sound different from *aa*.

blocks.caption: A vowel's magnitude spectrum: the thin lines are harmonics (source detail), the smooth curve is the envelope (filter). The humps in the envelope are formants F1, F2, F3. Hover any part.

blocks.prompt: You see a plot with time left to right, frequency bottom to top, and dark bands. What is it?
blocks.answer: A spectrogram. The dark bands are formants.

rows: where the wave starts in its cycle
the evenly spaced waves in a vowel; the lowest is F₀ (pitch)
the bumps from the mouth shape; tell vowels apart
blocks.title: Words from this chapter

exercises.title: Read the formula out loud
exercises.prompt: x(t) = 0.5 · cos(2π · 200 · t − π/2). What are A, F (in Hz), the period in ms, and ϕ?
hints: The number in front is A.
The number right before t is F. Then T = 1/F.
The number added at the end is ϕ.
exercises.why: Every lab question about a wave starts with reading these three numbers correctly.

exercises.title: Decibels without a calculator
exercises.prompt: Sound A has amplitude 10 times sound B. Sound C has amplitude 100 times B. How many dB is A above B? C above B?
hints: ×10 in amplitude is one of the two facts to memorize.
×100 = ×10 then ×10 again. Each ×10 adds 20 dB.
So add 20 twice.
exercises.why: Decibels show up on every audio meter and in every spectrum plot's y-axis.

exercises.title: Fill in: period from frequency
exercises.prompt: A wave has F = 50 Hz. Its period T is ____ seconds.
hints: 0.02 s, which is 20 ms.
exercises.why: Period and frequency are the first thing every lab asks you to read off a plot.

exercises.title: Fill in: frequency from period
exercises.prompt: One repeat of a wave takes 0.004 s. Its frequency is ____ Hz.
exercises.why: You'll convert between these constantly: pitch trackers report Hz, waveforms show you seconds.

exercises.title: Which dial?
exercises.prompt: In 3·cos(2π·5·t + π), which number is the amplitude?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: Amplitude = the number multiplying the cosine = 3.
exercises.why: Reading the three dials correctly is the first step of every Lab 3 question.

choices.feedback: Right: the number in front sets how tall the wave is.
2π is just 'one lap'; it's in every sinusoid.

exercises.title: What happens if…
exercises.prompt: You change 2·cos(2π·100·t) to 2·cos(2π·200·t). What happens to the plot?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: Only F changed, from 100 Hz to 200 Hz: twice as many cycles, each half as long.
exercises.why: Predicting the plot from the formula is Lab 3 Q2.

choices.text: Twice as many repeats per second (squished sideways)
choices.feedback: Right: F doubled, so the period halved (10 ms → 5 ms).
Starting point is ϕ, which stayed 0.

exercises.title: Decibels
exercises.prompt: Sound B's amplitude is twice sound A's. How much louder is B?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
exercises.why: Audio meters, spec sheets and spectrum plots are all in dB.

choices.feedback: dB don't add the ratio directly; it's 20·log₁₀(2) ≈ 6.
dB is a log scale; ×2 is always +6 dB, whatever the starting level.

exercises.title: Which plot?
exercises.prompt: Time goes left to right, frequency bottom to top, darkness shows strength. What is it?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: Time on x, frequency on y, darkness = amplitude: a spectrogram.
exercises.why: Spectrograms are the main picture in phonetics and in every speech tool.

choices.feedback: Right: a spectrum for every moment, side by side.
A waveform has pressure (not frequency) on the vertical axis.
A spectrum has frequency on the horizontal axis and no time axis.
Phase plots show angle against frequency.
